items_missed: The customer gave her name in her first sentence — 'Hi, this is Kirsten' — and Sergio never used it, never confirmed it, and never referenced it again across the entire call. He also never gave his own name until she asked for it at the very end: 'What was your name?'
Never asked how she was.
No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' The call goes from the greeting straight to 'This is the one coming from 7346 Stone Pine Lane, and are we moving the full home there or just some items?'

The destination was never captured beyond a town name. 'We're going to the Tomball, correct?' is the entire destination discovery on a job carrying a $105 trip fee — no street address, no zip, no confirmation of whether it is a house, a townhome, or an apartment, and no check on what floor anything lands on beyond the customer volunteering 'it would be just going to the first floor of the house, no stairs.'
Packing needs never asked. She said she and her husband are handling most of the move themselves; whether she wants any wrapping or packing help was never raised.

Special considerations never probed. On a job whose defining item is a large arcade cabinet, nobody asked about doorway width, hallway turns, or the path from the garage to the truck — the three things most likely to turn a two-and-a-half-hour move into a four-hour one.
Storage stops and additional stops never asked.
Access concerns never probed at either end — no parking, no driveway, no gate, no HOA, on a next-day move where there is no time to discover a problem later.

The moving-stressor question was never asked, and she signalled twice. 'I should probably ask just to be safe ask my husband cause I don't ever do this' is a first-time-mover hesitation and a second-decision-maker flag in one sentence, and it drew 'I can lock you in if you're interested.'
The 'pricing is super simple' opener was replaced with 'so yeah, to break down for pricing and stuff. Essentially...'

The what's-included list is completely absent. Not gas, not the truck, not taxes, not insurance, not wrap, not pads, not bands, not tools. The customer heard a rate, a trip fee and a minimum, and nothing about what she gets for it. This is the largest single gap on the call and it is the one that makes Einstein look like a commodity against the other quotes she said she had collected.

Disassembly and reassembly never mentioned — on a job consisting of a bed frame and an arcade cabinet, both of which are disassembly candidates, and on a call where she was already worried about whether the arcade could be moved at all.
No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. The signature item is an arcade cabinet with a screen in it.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, despite him giving her an arrival window ('an afternoon start window, it looks like between 12:00 and 2:00 PM') that she specifically asked about.
No no-hidden-fees pitch of any kind.

The clock explanation is one line long. 'We do have a two and a half hour minimum' is the entire section — no statement of when billable time starts, no mention of fifteen-minute prorated increments after the minimum, and no sense-check. The customer booked a move without knowing how she will be billed past the minimum.

The estimate was delivered as a single top-of-range number with the bottom hidden. At $102 per mover per hour with two movers plus a $105 trip fee, two and a half hours is $615 and three hours is $717. Sergio said 'I'll probably keep around a two and a half to three hour range for the move, essentially an estimate around $717 to get it completed' — he stated the range and then quoted only its ceiling. She replied 'I don't think that's bad at all' and booked against $717, never having heard that the floor is $615 and never having been told she only pays for time used. The quiet version of padding is quoting the top of your own range as the number.

The arcade — the one genuine unknown on the job — was never resolved before the quote. Sergio raised the right concerns twice ('do you know if the arcade can be moved with two guys?', 'we do have a weight limit of 350 for anything that goes upstairs') and then priced the move anyway without knowing its size, weight, or whether it needs disassembly. The customer offered to send a photo and he deferred it to after the booking email.
Walk distance never asked, no equivalents or plain-language anchors used, and no assembly or disassembly time factored into the estimate.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — a total zero on a next-day move, where prep matters more than on any other call type because there is no second chance to do it. And the customer teed it up herself: 'everything else we were just gonna move on our own, it's very little stuff.' She is already doing the carload strategy and got no reinforcement, no consolidation tips, and no 'here's what to have ready when the crew pulls up tomorrow.'

The no-deposit differentiator was delivered so badly it became an objection. Asked to book, Sergio said 'if you are interested we require deposit or, or credit card information' — the opposite of the actual policy. The customer, reasonably alarmed, asked 'Okay, so you need a credit card right now?', then 'Okay, and what's the deposit?', then a third time 'Or did you say there's no deposit? I'm sorry.' It took three rounds of correction to land Einstein's single strongest booking differentiator, and she ended up apologizing for his error.

No bolded-details framing on the confirmation email, and no reply-with-corrections verification ask. He did ask her to reply with the arcade reference, which is a request for information he is missing, not a request to verify what he has — and on a next-day move built from an unconfirmed destination address, a trip fee, and an unresolved arcade, the verification ask is the one that matters.

She asked a direct question — 'How do I get back in contact with you?' — and it was never answered. The reply was 'I can lock you in if you're interested.' No hours, no callback number, no name until she asked for it herself at the close.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?'
Customer's name used zero times.
top_strength: Sergio's instincts on the one genuinely risky item in this job were better than anyone else's in this week's sample, and he raised them unprompted. The customer mentioned an arcade cabinet almost in passing and he immediately went after the two things that actually determine whether it can be moved — crew size and weight: 'do you know if the arcade can be moved with two guys?' and then 'Is it like a pinball machine or is it... what is it?' When she could not describe it, he did not guess and he did not drop it — he asked for a photo: 'Are you able to text the machine to this phone number?' And when she said she could not get to it until five or six, he kept the door open rather than letting it die: 'that would work. Yeah, cool.' He then volunteered a hard operational constraint that most reps would never surface on a first call, and surfaced it at exactly the moment it became relevant — she had just said she was not sure whether the arcade was going to the garage or the second floor: 'we do have a weight limit of 350 for anything that goes upstairs, not sure if you know the weight of it, but yeah, if you could find a reference online that would help out.' That single sentence let the customer solve the problem herself in real time — 'Okay. I'm sure we can put it in the garage' — and it removed a day-of failure from a move happening in less than twenty-four hours. He also followed through on it at the close rather than letting it slide: 'once you get the email if you can respond back with the arcade machine reference and that would help out.' Two other things worth crediting. He scoped the job correctly at the open with a question that saves five minutes of wrong assumptions — 'are we moving the full home there or just some items?' — which is the right first question on a lead form and got him straight to the real answer ('it's actually just basically a master bedroom'). And when the customer hesitated, he made the most direct booking ask on any call this week: 'I can lock you in if you're interested.' Six words, no hedging, and it worked — she left the call booked for the next afternoon on what she herself called the best of the quotes she had collected.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is not subtle: fix the no-deposit answer. Asked to book, Sergio said 'if you are interested we require deposit or, or credit card information' — which is backwards, and it turned Einstein's strongest closing differentiator into an objection the customer had to dig him out of. She asked three separate times ('so you need a credit card right now?', 'what's the deposit?', 'Or did you say there's no deposit? I'm sorry') and ended up apologizing for his mistake. This one is a scripting drill, not a judgment call: 'There's no deposit and no card on file — you pay when the move is done, and if you need to cancel or move the date there's no fee. That's why locking it in costs you nothing.' He got there eventually, and the customer booked anyway, but on a less patient customer that exchange loses the sale outright. Second priority: there is no value story on this call at all. Not one word about what is included in the rate — no gas, no truck, no taxes, no insurance, no wrap, no pads, no tools, no disassembly and reassembly, no No Worries Damage Coverage, no On-Time Guarantee, no Meet Your Mover, no no-hidden-fees pitch. The customer said 'from the other quotes I got this is definitely the best option,' which means she is comparing Einstein to competitors on price alone, because price is the only thing she was given. She is moving an arcade cabinet with a screen in it; thirty seconds on No Worries Damage Coverage is the difference between winning on value and winning on being cheapest, and winning on cheapest is how a branch ends up defending its rate later. Third, the clock section was one sentence. The two-and-a-half-hour minimum was stated and the fifteen-minute proration was not, which means she booked a move not knowing how the time past the minimum is billed — and on a job where the arcade is still an unknown, the odds of going past the minimum are real. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-four review, and this is the padding pattern in its quietest form: Sergio stated the range as 'two and a half to three hour range' and then quoted a single number — '$717' — which is the three-hour ceiling, not the range. The floor is $615. She heard one number, the worst case, and never learned that she only pays for the time actually used. He also priced the job before resolving the only variable that could actually move it: he twice flagged that he did not know the arcade's size or weight, deferred the photo until after booking, and quoted anyway. The correct version is thirty seconds longer and materially more accurate: 'Two movers and a truck at $102 per mover per hour, plus the $105 trip fee to get back from Tomball. The minimum is two and a half hours, which puts you at $615, and if the drive and the arcade push it to three you're at $717 — you only pay for what we actually use. Send me that photo tonight and I'll tighten it up before tomorrow.' That is the same call, honestly bounded, and it also gets the photo before the crew rolls instead of after. Last: she asked 'How do I get back in contact with you?' and never got an answer — he pivoted to the booking ask instead. That is a direct customer question going unanswered on a move happening in under twenty-four hours, and she had to ask his name at the end of the call to know who she had spoken to. Name, direct number and office hours before hanging up, every time.
phone_presence_notes: Efficient but almost entirely transactional — the customer's name is never used once, his own name is not offered until she asks for it at the close, and the two clear emotional cues in the call both go unacknowledged: 'I should probably ask just to be safe, ask my husband cause I don't ever do this' draws a booking push rather than reassurance, and 'from the other quotes I got this is definitely the best option' draws no response at all; the deposit exchange then runs three confused rounds until the customer apologizes for his error, and the farewell is a bare 'Yeah, thank you. Bye-bye.'
audio_review_reason: Scored a 2, which the rubric flags automatically, and this transcript needs it more than most. Sergio's turns interleave badly out of sequence through the entire deposit exchange — his 'Yeah, sorry. Yeah, no, no, no deposit, no credit for it' lands before the customer's question it is answering, and several of his lines run together into one block ('Okay, yeah, yeah, I'll send it here in the next five minutes. Okay, and then.'). It is not possible to tell from text alone whether he genuinely contradicted himself on the deposit policy on the call or whether the transcription scrambled a clean correction, and that distinction decides whether this is a knowledge gap to coach or a transcript artifact to ignore. The clarity-and-pace deduction rests on the same evidence.
